newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 21.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Monday:

* News Analysis: U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan seemed to indicate in December that the stock market boom was coming to a close. Now, it appears he meant that the speculative frenzy that could foreshadow a market slump has not come yet.
* AT&T's strategy to expand its global reach seems to be coming apart, while the international pact between MCI Communications and British Telecommunications has gained strength.
* More than 12,000 U.S. union employees of Goodyear Tire went on strike at nine plants after negotiators were unable to reach agreement on a new three-year contract.
* An advertising industry group has developed voluntary guidelines for marketing to children on the Internet.
* The liberal-oriented Nation magazine has sent out brochures seeking donations for itself.
* Publishing, research and trade-show concern International Data Group views itself as the Procter & Gamble of the technology media marketplace.
* President Clinton's trip to South Carolina in December was a key moment in the complex steps that led to talks among tobacco companies, regulators and anti-smoking advocates.
* Surprisingly little is known about who is using the Web and how they are using it.
* Researchers are developing computer systems programmed to speak a particular person's voice.
* Executive shifts at Creative Artists and William Morris have created turbulence in the talent agency business.
* The remote control has become a sophisticated tool to operate VCRs, laser disk players and digital video disk devices.
* A new competitor in high-quality big-screen televisions, based on Texas Instruments technology, has entered the market.
* Advertising: Internet Shopper magazine reviews Internet sites that sell everything from imported olive oil to flight reservations.
* Authors of the best-selling book "Sisters" could be poised for a battle with their brother-in-law and former publisher over books on mothers and daughters.
